strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated and conceptually clear reframing of self-supervised NVS around 'transferability' — the idea that pose latents should induce the same trajectory across different scenes — which cleanly explains why prior geometry-free methods (RayZer, RUST) actually behave as context-frame interpolators rather than true view synthesizers.

The proposed True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric operationalizes this criterion in a simple, reusable way and is applied consistently across four diverse, large-scale real-world datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2), giving the empirical claims decent breadth.

The stereo-monocular bootstrapping idea (forcing extrapolation rather than interpolation) combined with the pose-preserving augmentation/masking scheme for constructing pseudo-pairs from single sequences is a simple but effective technical contribution that plausibly explains the large empirical gains.

Results show large, consistent margins over re-implemented RayZer and RUST baselines on the transferability metric and pose-probing experiments, and the paper is transparent about re-implementation choices (e.g., sharing the RayZer re-implementation with its authors for validation).

The ablation study is thorough and includes a genuinely counter-intuitive and informative finding: explicit SE(3)/Plücker parameterization of poses hurts transferability relative to an unconstrained latent, which is a useful negative result for the community.
Architecture and training details are reasonably well documented in the appendix, aiding reproducibility despite the absence of official baseline code.
weaknesses: The evaluation's ground truth is itself a learned model (VGGT) rather than true ground-truth camera parameters or COLMAP outputs for all datasets; since XFactor's success is measured entirely relative to this pseudo-oracle, there is a risk of circularity or oracle-specific bias affecting both TPS and probe results, and no validation of oracle accuracy/consistency across datasets is provided.

Both baselines (RayZer, RUST) are re-implemented from scratch due to lack of public code; although the RayZer re-implementation was reportedly validated by its authors, RUST's implementation is explicitly described as differing from the original design (no set-latent scene representation, absorbed scene encoder), which somewhat weakens the fairness/strength of that comparison and could inflate the apparent margin.

The practical significance of 'transferability' as defined (applying poses extracted from one arbitrary scene to a completely different scene, ignoring intrinsics/scale differences) is not clearly justified beyond a diagnostic/representation-learning value; it's unclear how useful literal pose transfer across unrelated scenes is for real applications compared to standard pose-conditioned rendering.

FID is used as the main 'general measure of transferred rendering quality,' but this is a coarse, distribution-level metric not well suited to assessing per-instance faithfulness of individual transferred renders; the paper itself acknowledges TPS can be 'hacked' and needs pairing with a faithfulness measure, yet the faithfulness evaluation offered (FID, qualitative examples) is comparatively weak.

The method inherits an architectural limitation (stereo-only pose encoder) that precludes handling wide-baseline/multi-view context robustly in a single pass, an issue explicitly acknowledged but left unresolved, limiting the scope of applicability relative to true multi-view geometric pipelines.

Blurring/warping artifacts in transferred renders when target poses diverge substantially from context are noted but not quantitatively characterized (e.g., no breakdown of quality vs. pose divergence), leaving open how severe this degradation is in practice.

No comparison to more recent or stronger geometry-aware self-supervised baselines beyond RayZer and RUST, and no discussion of computational cost/efficiency trade-offs relative to baselines despite using substantial compute (multiple H200 GPUs for tens of hours).

strengths: The paper introduces a clear, useful conceptual framing (transferability) that meaningfully distinguishes true novel view synthesis from frame interpolation in self-supervised settings, which is a valuable diagnostic for the community.
The proposed True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric is well formalized and directly operationalizes the transferability concept, enabling quantitative comparison across methods.

The ablation studies (Table 3) are fairly comprehensive, isolating the effects of stereo-monocular vs. multi-view training and different pose parameterizations (bottleneck, SE(3)+Plucker, unconstrained), yielding an interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive finding that explicit SE(3) parameterization hurts transferability.
Experiments span four diverse, large-scale real-world datasets (scene- and object-level), and probing experiments provide additional evidence that the learned latents correlate with real-world poses.
The paper is generally clearly written and the latent-variable formalization in Section 3.1 provides a useful unifying lens for comparing oracle-based and self-supervised NVS methods.
weaknesses: Both baselines (RayZer and RUST) are self-reimplemented since no official code exists; while the authors state RayZer's authors confirmed fidelity, the RUST reimplementation is explicitly acknowledged to differ substantially from the original design (e.g., no set-latent scene representation), weakening confidence that the comparison is fair to the actual published methods and raising reproducibility concerns.

The proposed TPS metric is explicitly acknowledged to not measure faithfulness to the context scene and can be 'hacked'; the paper does not propose or use a joint metric capturing both transferability and faithfulness, which undercuts the strength of the central 'true NVS' claims.

The core technical contribution (restricting to stereo-monocular training to avoid interpolation shortcuts, plus masking-based augmentation to prevent pixel-content leakage) is a relatively incremental combination of existing representation-learning ideas (e.g., CroCo-style masking, information bottlenecks), limiting the technical novelty beyond the conceptual framing.

The claim of having 'no 3D inductive biases whatsoever' is overstated: the choice of pose-preserving augmentations (Eq. 12) and the stereo-pair structure of training implicitly encode geometric knowledge about what constitutes pose-preserving transformations, which is itself a form of inductive bias in the training pipeline.

Ablation results show that simpler baselines (e.g., the bottlenecked or unconstrained stereo-monocular model) are sometimes competitive with or even slightly better than full XFactor on some transferability metrics (e.g., MVImgNet AUC@20°), somewhat undermining the narrative that the full proposed recipe is uniformly best.

The method is restricted to pairwise/stereo pose estimation and explicitly cannot handle ultra-wide baselines in a single pass; combined with acknowledged blurring/warping artifacts at larger pose divergence, this limits the practical significance of the claimed 'true NVS' capability.

No comparison to oracle-based state-of-the-art methods (e.g., LVSM, pixelSplat) is provided to contextualize how far the self-supervised results are from an upper bound, and no code/data release is confirmed, limiting reproducibility and ability to calibrate significance.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually novel and useful criterion for self-supervised NVS: transferability, i.e., that pose latents extracted in one scene should induce the same camera trajectory when applied to render a different scene. This reframes NVS evaluation in a way that exposes a real failure mode (interpolation masquerading as view synthesis) in prior self-supervised methods.

Proposes a new, well-motivated evaluation metric (TPS) built on top of oracle SE(3) trajectories and standard geometric accuracy measures, and is careful to note its limitations (it must be paired with a perceptual/faithfulness metric).

The method (stereo-monocular bootstrapping + pose-preserving augmentation + explicit transferability objective) is simple, clearly motivated by two concrete failure modes (interpolation and information leakage), and is described with sufficient architectural detail (Appendix A) to be largely reproducible.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four diverse, large-scale real-world datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2) at both scene and object level, with consistent large margins over two representative self-supervised baselines (RayZer, RUST) on the transferability metric.

Thorough and informative ablations that isolate the contribution of the stereo-monocular design vs. multi-view training, and the transferability objective vs. standard autoencoding, including a genuinely counter-intuitive and useful finding that explicit SE(3)/Plücker parameterization hurts rather than helps transferability.
Pose-probe experiments provide complementary evidence that the learned latents are correlated with real-world poses, strengthening the overall narrative beyond the primary transfer metric.
Honest discussion of limitations (restriction to stereo pose estimation, rendering artifacts under large pose divergence, deterministic vs. generative modeling).
weaknesses: The individual technical components (masked/inverse-augmented image pairs reminiscent of CroCo-style cross-view completion, stereo bootstrapping to avoid interpolation, transferability-style contrastive-like objectives) are each fairly close to existing ideas in self-supervised representation learning; the core novelty lies mainly in their combination and framing rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Reproducibility is a concern: neither RayZer nor RUST have public code, and the paper relies on its own reimplementations (with RayZer confirmed by original authors, but RUST explicitly noted as differing from the original in the scene-representation design). This makes some baseline comparisons somewhat uncertain and not fully apples-to-apples, and no code is released for XFactor itself as far as the manuscript indicates.

The evaluation depends heavily on VGGT as the pose oracle for both computing the TPS metric and probing; any systematic bias or failure modes of VGGT could propagate into the reported transferability numbers, and this potential circularity/bias is not discussed or validated against an independent oracle (e.g., COLMAP) for cross-checking.

In the ablations (Table 3), the "Unconstrained" stereo-monocular model trained with the plain autoencoding objective already achieves transfer numbers fairly close to full XFactor (e.g., R 20°: 99.8 vs 99.9), suggesting that much of the benefit comes from the stereo-monocular restriction itself rather than the proposed transferability objective; the paper does not sufficiently discuss how much incremental value the explicit transferability loss provides beyond the architectural bottleneck.

Acknowledged rendering-quality degradation (blur/warping) for target poses that diverge substantially from context, which limits the practical usefulness of the method for genuinely novel (far-from-context) viewpoints — arguably the most important use case for NVS.

The model is restricted to a stereo (pairwise) pose encoder, precluding single-pass wide-baseline pose estimation; the extension to a more capable multi-view pose encoder is left as future/open work, limiting the immediate practical impact relative to state-of-the-art supervised methods like VGGT.

Autoencoding reconstruction results (Table 4, Appendix B) show XFactor and RayZer are fairly close in raw perceptual quality despite the large gap in transferability, which somewhat tempers the practical significance of the transferability gains if end users mainly care about visual fidelity in typical (non-adversarial) settings.

No user study or downstream task evaluation (e.g., 3D reconstruction, robotics, or other applications) is provided to demonstrate practical significance of transferable poses beyond the introduced metric and probing analysis.

strengths: Introduces a clear, well-motivated, and novel conceptual criterion (transferability) for what constitutes 'true' novel view synthesis in the self-supervised setting, formalized rigorously as a property of latent-variable NVS models.

Proposes a principled new metric (True Pose Similarity) to quantify transferability, with clear derivation and discussion of its limitations (e.g., that it must be paired with a perceptual/faithfulness measure).

Convincingly diagnoses why prior self-supervised methods (RayZer, RUST) fail to be truly controllable NVS models — i.e., they learn to interpolate context frames rather than reason geometrically — and supports this claim with strong empirical evidence (dramatic TPS gaps in Table 1) and qualitative trajectory visualizations.

The proposed method (XFactor) is simple and well-motivated: bootstrapping a stereo-monocular extrapolation model plus a transferability training objective realized via pose-preserving augmentations, avoiding explicit SE(3)/3D inductive biases.

Extensive empirical validation across four diverse large-scale real-world datasets (scene- and object-level), with thorough ablations isolating the effects of stereo-monocular vs multi-view training and unconstrained vs SE(3)-constrained pose representations, yielding a counter-intuitive but well-supported finding that explicit SE(3) parameterization hurts transferability.

Very thorough appendix: robustness checks of the oracle (VGGT vs COLMAP) used for evaluation, comparisons against generic self-supervised objectives (SimCLR, VICReg), robustness of the training objective under corrupted pairing, and comparisons of autoencoding vs true transfer performance, and honest discussion of limitations (wide-baseline pose estimation, blurring artifacts, comparison to supervised LVSM under similar difficulty).

Pose-probing experiments show that XFactor's unconstrained latent poses correlate strongly with ground-truth SE(3) poses despite no explicit geometric parameterization, supporting the paper's central thesis that inductive bias is not necessary for geometric reasoning to emerge.
weaknesses: The core architectural contribution (stereo-monocular bootstrapping + input/output augmentation for pose-preserving pixel-content separation) is relatively simple engineering built on existing ideas (e.g., CroCo-style monocular decoding, standard masking/augmentation strategies), with the main novelty residing in the framing/diagnosis (transferability) rather than fundamentally new architecture or learning mechanism.

Baseline reimplementations of RayZer and RUST are necessary since no official code is released, and although the authors report validation from RayZer's authors, subtle implementation differences (losses, dataset mixing, iteration budgets, number of context views) could affect the fairness or generalizability of the comparison, as acknowledged by discrepancies with originally reported numbers.

The stereo-only pose encoder architecturally precludes single-pass wide-baseline pose estimation, an important practical limitation for scaling to sparse-view or long-sequence settings, which is only partially addressed as a stated 'open problem' rather than resolved.

Rendered outputs for wide-baseline/out-of-distribution target poses still exhibit noticeable blurring/warping artifacts, and while the authors note that supervised methods (LVSM) also suffer similarly, this somewhat weakens claims of practical high-quality NVS performance.

The TPS metric, as explicitly acknowledged by the authors, can be 'hacked' by models that ignore transferred poses and instead reproduce autoencoding behavior, meaning transferability alone is not a complete measure of true NVS quality and must be interpreted alongside FID/perceptual metrics, adding some ambiguity to how conclusively transferability can be judged from the reported numbers alone.

Limited comparison scope: recent related unposed/geometry-light methods mentioned in related work (e.g., Less3Depend, SelfSplat) are not empirically compared against, leaving open whether XFactor's gains are specific to RayZer/RUST-style architectures or would generalize across the broader landscape of self-supervised NVS approaches.
